claim: The structure of HIV-1 TAR in complex with HIV-1 Tat and human AFF4, CDK9, and CycT1 was determined at 5.9 Å resolution.
source: Here we report the 5.9 Å structure of HIV-1 TAR in complex with HIV-1 Tat and human AFF4, CDK9, and CycT1.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution of the crystal structure determined in this study.

claim: The TAR central loop contacts the CycT1 Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM).
source: The TAR central loop contacts the CycT1 Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM) and the second Tat Zn2+-binding loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The TAR central loop contacts the second Tat Zn2+-binding loop.
source: The TAR central loop contacts the CycT1 Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM) and the second Tat Zn2+-binding loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: AFF4 helix 2 is stabilized in the TAR complex despite not touching the RNA.
source: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange (HDX) shows that AFF4 helix 2 is stabilized in the TAR complex despite not touching the RNA, explaining how it enhances TAR binding to the SEC 50-fold.
evidence: HDX data shows protection of AFF4 helix 2 upon TAR binding, and the crystal structure shows no direct contact between AFF4 and TAR.

claim: AFF4 enhances TAR binding to the SEC 50-fold.
source: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange (HDX) shows that AFF4 helix 2 is stabilized in the TAR complex despite not touching the RNA, explaining how it enhances TAR binding to the SEC 50-fold.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by binding assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Tat Arginine-Rich Motif (ARM) enters the TAR major groove between the bulge and the central loop.
source: RNA SHAPE and SAXS data were used to help model the extended (Tat Arginine-Rich Motif) ARM, which enters the TAR major groove between the bulge and the central loop.
evidence: This is based on integrative modeling using SHAPE, SAXS, and the crystal structure as constraints.

claim: The TAR central loop engages the CycT1 TRM and compact core of Tat.
source: The structure and functional assays collectively support an integrative structure and a bipartite binding model, wherein the TAR central loop engages the CycT1 TRM and compact core of Tat, while the TAR major groove interacts with the extended Tat ARM.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the structural and functional data.

claim: The TAR major groove interacts with the extended Tat ARM.
source: The structure and functional assays collectively support an integrative structure and a bipartite binding model, wherein the TAR central loop engages the CycT1 TRM and compact core of Tat, while the TAR major groove interacts with the extended Tat ARM.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the structural and functional data.

claim: HIV-1 remains one of the world's leading health threats.
source: The human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) remains one of the world's leading health threats.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HIV-1.

claim: It has not been possible to eradicate HIV-1 infection despite advances in treatment with antiretrovirals (HAART).
source: In spite of advances in treatment with antiretrovirals (HAART) (Yeni 2006), it has not been possible to eradicate HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Resting T cells that harbor latent provirus integrated into their genome survive even under intensive antiretroviral therapy.
source: Even under intensive antiretroviral therapy, resting T cells that harbor latent provirus integrated into their genome survive (Archin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The pool of latent virus is the primary obstacle to eradicating HIV.
source: The pool of latent virus is the primary obstacle to eradicating HIV, and thus the mechanisms by which latency is regulated are of paramount interest.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Proviral transcription is silenced by host epigenetic mechanisms and/or deficiency in key cofactors.
source: Proviral transcription is silenced by host epigenetic mechanisms and/or deficiency in key cofactors, and is reactivated at the level of both initiation and elongation (Mbonye and Karn 2014; Zhou et al., 2012; Jonkers and Lis 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Proviral transcription is reactivated at the level of both initiation and elongation.
source: Proviral transcription is silenced by host epigenetic mechanisms and/or deficiency in key cofactors, and is reactivated at the level of both initiation and elongation (Mbonye and Karn 2014; Zhou et al., 2012; Jonkers and Lis 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Transcription of the HIV-1 proviral DNA is initiated by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) binding to the HIV promoter.
source: Transcription of the HIV-1 proviral DNA is initiated by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) binding to the HIV promoter, but stalls after a 30–50 nucleotide transcript containing the trans-activation response region (TAR) is formed.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HIV-1 transcription.

claim: RNA polymerase II stalls after a 30–50 nucleotide transcript containing the trans-activation response region (TAR) is formed.
source: Transcription of the HIV-1 proviral DNA is initiated by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) binding to the HIV promoter, but stalls after a 30–50 nucleotide transcript containing the trans-activation response region (TAR) is formed.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HIV-1 transcription.

claim: Release of the stalled Pol II is dependent on the recruitment of the host super elongation complex (SEC) to the nascent TAR by HIV-1 trans-activator protein (Tat).
source: Release of the stalled Pol II is dependent on the recruitment of the host super elongation complex (SEC) (He et al., 2010; Sobhian et al., 2010) to the nascent TAR by HIV-1 trans-activator protein (Tat), a central driver of proviral transcriptional activation (Fisher et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: HIV-1 Tat is a central driver of proviral transcriptional activation.
source: Release of the stalled Pol II is dependent on the recruitment of the host super elongation complex (SEC) (He et al., 2010; Sobhian et al., 2010) to the nascent TAR by HIV-1 trans-activator protein (Tat), a central driver of proviral transcriptional activation (Fisher et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The SEC is assembled on the AFF1 or AFF4 scaffold protein.
source: The SEC is assembled on the AFF1 or AFF4 scaffold protein that interacts through small binding domains with the positive elongation factor b (P-TEFb), composed of CDK9 and Cyclin T1 (CycT1), the transcription factor ELL1/ELL2, and ENL/AF9 (Chou et al., 2013; He et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010; Sobhian et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: P-TEFb is composed of CDK9 and Cyclin T1 (CycT1).
source: The SEC is assembled on the AFF1 or AFF4 scaffold protein that interacts through small binding domains with the positive elongation factor b (P-TEFb), composed of CDK9 and Cyclin T1 (CycT1), the transcription factor ELL1/ELL2, and ENL/AF9 (Chou et al., 2013; He et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010; Sobhian et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: P-TEFb facilitates promoter escape by phosphorylating two negative elongation factors (DSIF and NELF) as well as the C-terminal domain of Pol II.
source: P-TEFb facilitates promoter escape by phosphorylating two negative elongation factors (DSIF and NELF) as well as the C-terminal domain of Pol II.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about P-TEFb function.

claim: Overexpression of full-length AFF1 strongly increases Tat transactivation of transcription from the HIV promoter.
source: Overexpression of full-length AFF1, but not a fragment that only binds to P-TEFb, strongly increases Tat transactivation of transcription from the HIV promoter (Lu et al., 2014), indicating that productive HIV transcription requires the whole SEC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Overexpression of an AFF1 fragment that only binds to P-TEFb does not strongly increase Tat transactivation of transcription from the HIV promoter.
source: Overexpression of full-length AFF1, but not a fragment that only binds to P-TEFb, strongly increases Tat transactivation of transcription from the HIV promoter (Lu et al., 2014), indicating that productive HIV transcription requires the whole SEC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Productive HIV transcription requires the whole SEC.
source: Overexpression of full-length AFF1, but not a fragment that only binds to P-TEFb, strongly increases Tat transactivation of transcription from the HIV promoter (Lu et al., 2014), indicating that productive HIV transcription requires the whole SEC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental data.

claim: The intrinsically disordered P-TEFb-binding domain of AFF4 folds and binds in a hydrophobic groove on the CycT1 surface.
source: Recent crystal structures have revealed how the intrinsically disordered P-TEFb-binding domain of AFF4 folds and binds in a hydrophobic groove on the CycT1 surface (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2013; Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: HIV-1 Tat binds to CycT1 in an extended conformation adjacent to AFF4.
source: HIV-1 Tat binds to CycT1 in an extended conformation adjacent to AFF4, interacting with residues in the cleft between the two cyclin-fold domains of CycT1, the Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM), and AFF4 helix α2 (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014; Tahirov et al., 2010; Gu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: HIV-1 Tat interacts with residues in the cleft between the two cyclin-fold domains of CycT1, the Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM), and AFF4 helix α2.
source: HIV-1 Tat binds to CycT1 in an extended conformation adjacent to AFF4, interacting with residues in the cleft between the two cyclin-fold domains of CycT1, the Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM), and AFF4 helix α2 (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014; Tahirov et al., 2010; Gu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: Segments from AFF4, Tat, and CycT1 TRM that are flexible in isolation come together to form a more stable structure with a positively charged surface.
source: Segments from AFF4, Tat, and CycT1 TRM that are flexible in isolation come together to form a more stable structure with a positively charged surface (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Both Tat and CycT1 make critical and direct contributions to TAR binding.
source: Biochemical experiments have shown that both Tat and CycT1 make critical and direct contributions to TAR binding (Calnan et al., 1991; Richter et al., 2002b; Garber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: In the presence of AFF4, TAR affinity to P-TEFb increases sharply.
source: In the presence of AFF4, TAR affinity to P-TEFb increases sharply (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The C-terminal segment (residues 59-67) of the synthetic AFF4 peptide (32–67) shows 70% deuteration after 10 s and almost complete deuteration within 3 min.
source: The C-terminal segment (residues 59-67) of the synthetic AFF4 peptide (32–67) shows 70% deuteration after 10 s and almost complete deuteration within 3 min (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM; residues 246 to 262 in CycT1) showed almost complete deuteration within 10 s in the apo complex.
source: The Tat-TAR recognition motif (TRM; residues 246 to 262 in CycT1, (Das et al., 2004; Garber et al., 1998) also showed almost complete deuteration within 10 s in the apo complex (Figure 1B), which is consistent with multiple conformations for the TRM in the crystal structure (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Strong protection for the CycT1 TRM was observed after TAR binding compared with the apo complex.
source: Compared with the apo complex, we observed strong protection for the CycT1 TRM and AFF4 helix α2 (residues 59–65) after TAR binding (Figure 1B, dark blue segments) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Strong protection for AFF4 helix α2 (residues 59–65) was observed after TAR binding compared with the apo complex.
source: Compared with the apo complex, we observed strong protection for the CycT1 TRM and AFF4 helix α2 (residues 59–65) after TAR binding (Figure 1B, dark blue segments) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: The CycT1 TRM and AFF4 helix α2 are adjacent to each other in the crystal structure of Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb.
source: These two segments are adjacent to each other in the crystal structure of Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb, consistent with their mutual cooperation in forming the TAR binding site.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of the apo complex.

claim: Tat exhibited a lesser degree of protection compared to CycT1 and AFF4, localized to the N-terminal segment (residues 1-33).
source: In contrast to CycT1 and AFF4, Tat exhibited a lesser degree of protection, localized to the N-terminal segment (residues 1-33) (Figure 1B, light blue segments).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Tat ARM did not show any significant protection in HDX after TAR binding.
source: Surprisingly, the Tat ARM did not show any significant protection in HDX after TAR binding despite its well-established role in TAR binding (Weeks and Crothers, 1991; Calnan et al., 1991) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tat ARM–TAR interactions are mediated primarily by amino acid side chains, without extensive hydrogen bonding and solvent exclusion of main-chain amide protons.
source: This observation indicates that Tat ARM–TAR interactions are mediated primarily by amino acid side chains, without extensive hydrogen bonding and solvent exclusion of main-chain amide protons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the HDX data showing no protection of the Tat ARM.

claim: Upon protein complex binding, the major SHAPE changes cluster in the 5' TAR region of the 5'UTR.
source: Upon protein complex binding, the major SHAPE changes cluster in the 5' TAR region of the 5'UTR (Figure 2A,B) with significant SHAPE changes observed around the bulge region at A17, the bulge region A22-U25, as well as the loop region C30-A35.
evidence: This is based on SHAPE data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significant SHAPE changes were observed around the bulge region at A17, the bulge region A22-U25, as well as the loop region C30-A35 upon Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb binding.
source: Upon protein complex binding, the major SHAPE changes cluster in the 5' TAR region of the 5'UTR (Figure 2A,B) with significant SHAPE changes observed around the bulge region at A17, the bulge region A22-U25, as well as the loop region C30-A35.
evidence: This is based on SHAPE data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No significant reactivity changes were observed in the regions 3' to TAR upon Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb binding.
source: As expected, no significant reactivity changes were observed in the regions 3' to TAR.
evidence: This is based on SHAPE data.

claim: TAR binding reduces SHAPE reactivity by 0.3-0.4 for nucleotides in the bulge region.
source: TAR binding reduces SHAPE reactivity by 0.3-0.4 and 0.2-1.2 for nucleotides in the bulge and loop region, respectively.
evidence: This is based on SHAPE data.

claim: TAR binding reduces SHAPE reactivity by 0.2-1.2 for nucleotides in the loop region.
source: TAR binding reduces SHAPE reactivity by 0.3-0.4 and 0.2-1.2 for nucleotides in the bulge and loop region, respectively.
evidence: This is based on SHAPE data.

claim: The pattern of changes in SHAPE reactivity for TAR after binding the SEC is significantly different from changes observed after TAR binding to a Tat peptide covering the ARM region.
source: The pattern of changes in SHAPE reactivity for TAR after binding the SEC is significantly different from changes observed after TAR binding to a Tat peptide covering the ARM region (Kenyon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of SHAPE data with a cited study.

claim: Reduction in SHAPE activity correlates with reduced flexibility of the respective RNA regions.
source: Because reduction in SHAPE activity correlates with reduced flexibility of the respective RNA regions (McGinnis et al., 2012), the results for the TAR-SEC complex indicate a stabilization of the bulge and loop structure through direct contacts between TAR and the SEC (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SHAPE, supported by a citation.

claim: The results for the TAR-SEC complex indicate a stabilization of the bulge and loop structure through direct contacts between TAR and the SEC.
source: Because reduction in SHAPE activity correlates with reduced flexibility of the respective RNA regions (McGinnis et al., 2012), the results for the TAR-SEC complex indicate a stabilization of the bulge and loop structure through direct contacts between TAR and the SEC (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SHAPE data.

claim: The RG of the TAR complex increases by 2.8 Å upon TAR binding.
source: The RG of the TAR complex increases by 2.8 Å upon TAR binding.
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The Porod exponent is smaller for the TAR complex than the apo complex.
source: The Porod exponent, in contrast, is smaller for the TAR complex than the apo complex.
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The TAR complex appears slightly less compact than the apo structure.
source: The TAR complex appears slightly less compact than the apo structure, which agrees with the differences in the shape of the P(r) function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Porod exponent and P(r) function from SAXS data.

claim: The crystal structure of the TAR:Tat:SEC complex was solved at 5.9 Å resolution.
source: To clearly define the interactions between TAR and Tat:P-TEFb, and to determine if direct interactions existed between TAR and AFF4, we solved the crystal structure of the TAR:Tat:SEC complex at 5.9 Å resolution (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: The structure was solved by molecular replacement with one copy of the Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb complex (PDB ID 4OGR) in the asymmetric unit.
source: The structure was solved by molecular replacement with one copy of the Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb complex (PDB ID 4OGR) in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination.

claim: Strong density for the TAR RNA became visible in the Fo-Fc electron density map after rigid-body and torsion angle molecular dynamics refinement with deformable elastic network (DEN) restraints.
source: After rigid-body and torsion angle molecular dynamics refinement with deformable elastic network (DEN) restraints (Table 2) (Schröder et al., 2010; Brunger et al., 2012) strong density for the TAR RNA became visible in the Fo-Fc electron density map (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) which allowed placement of one TAR molecule (PDB ID 1ARJ) into the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This describes the crystallographic refinement process and is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The complex was refined to R/Rfree = 0.211/0.311 with good geometry.
source: The complex was further refined to R/Rfree = 0.211/0.311 with good geometry (Table 2) and an excellent fit to the density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the final refinement statistics.

claim: The extended TAR loop region 29-33 contributes the main interactions with the SEC.
source: The extended TAR loop region 29-33 contributes the main interactions with the SEC.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: TAR loop region 29-33 interacts with the protein complex surface composed of CycT1 TRM and the Tat cysteine-rich region, especially the Zn2+-coordinating loop (Tat 24-29).
source: It interacts with the protein complex surface composed of CycT1 TRM and the Tat cysteine-rich region, especially the Zn2+-coordinating loop (Tat 24-29).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: The crystal structure rules out direct interactions between TAR and AFF4 α2.
source: This structure rules out direct interactions between TAR and AFF4 α2.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure showing no contacts between TAR and AFF4.

claim: TAR loop nucleotides G32 and G33 abut the Tat Zn2+ -coordination loop (24-29) and CycT TRM, residues 259-261.
source: TAR loop nucleotides G32 and G33 abut the Tat Zn2+ -coordination loop (24-29) and CycT TRM, residues 259-261.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: The backbone phosphates of nucleotides 30–32 contact basic residues in the CycT TRM region.
source: The backbone phosphates of nucleotides 30–32 contact basic residues in the CycT TRM region (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: The N-terminus of the Tat ARM (Arg49) is positioned at the widest point in the TAR major groove, which is 13 Å wide between nucleobases C24 and G34.
source: This orientation places the N-terminus of the Tat ARM (Arg49) at the widest point in the TAR major groove, which is 13 Å wide between nucleobases C24 and G34.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: There is not interpretable electron density present for residues in the Tat ARM region at the limited resolution of this crystal structure.
source: However, there is not interpretable electron density present for residues in the Tat ARM region at the limited resolution of this crystal structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the crystal structure.

claim: The structure of the TAR complex with Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb shows no direct contacts between AFF4 and TAR.
source: The structure of the TAR complex with Tat:AFF4:P-TEFb shows no direct contacts between AFF4 and TAR.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: AFF4 helix α2 and its N-terminal loop connection to helix α1 are interacting with CycT1 TRM and Tat helix α1.
source: Instead, AFF4 helix α2 and its N-terminal loop connection to helix α1 are interacting with CycT1 TRM and Tat helix α1.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure.

claim: The interaction network between AFF4 helix α2, CycT1 TRM, and Tat helix α1 most likely stabilizes the protein interaction surface for TAR and indirectly increases Tat:SEC affinity for TAR in the presence of AFF4.
source: The interaction network between these three protein regions most likely stabilizes the protein interaction surface for TAR and indirectly increases Tat:SEC affinity for TAR in the presence of AFF4 (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crystal structure and previous binding data.

claim: Five best scoring clusters of Tat ARM and CycT1 TRM models were obtained with precisions between 2.5 and 6.3 Å.
source: Using hierarchical clustering and DOPE scoring (Shen and Sali, 2006) we obtained five best scoring clusters with precisions between 2.5 and 6.3 Å (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: The computed small angle scattering fits well with SAXS data obtained from the TAR complex in solution with χ=0.86.
source: The computed small angle scattering fits well with SAXS data obtained from the TAR complex in solution with χ=0.86 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model with experimental SAXS data.

claim: The CycT1 TRM segment is anchored by CycT1 Cys261, which coordinates one of the Tat Zn2+ ions.
source: The CycT1 TRM segment is anchored by CycT1 Cys261, which coordinates one of the Tat Zn2+ ions and displays structural variability in the center part of the TRM (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on the modeled structures shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Tat ARM region is N-terminally anchored by Tat Tyr47, which binds to a pocket on the CycT1 surface and interacts with CycT1 residues Leu44, Asp47, and Cys111.
source: The Tat ARM region is N-terminally anchored by Tat Tyr47, which binds to a pocket on the CycT1 surface and interacts with CycT1 residues Leu44, Asp47, and Cys111 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on the modeled structures shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ARM (residues 49-57) extends into the major groove of TAR stretching from the TAR bulge towards the phosphate backbone opposite the bulge.
source: From there, the ARM (residues 49-57) extends into the major groove of TAR stretching from the TAR bulge towards the phosphate backbone opposite the bulge.
evidence: This is based on the modeled structures.

claim: Basic side chains in the Tat ARM are in positions where they can form previously described interactions with the TAR G26 nucleobase, and phosphates P22, P23, and P40 in the TAR backbone.
source: Basic side chains in the Tat ARM are in positions where they can form previously described interactions with the TAR G26 nucleobase, and phosphates P22, P23, and P40 in the TAR backbone (Puglisi et al., 1993; Aboul-ela et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on the modeled structures and comparison with previously published data.

claim: The single site mutant AFF4 E61A shows a three-fold reduction in TAR binding.
source: The single site mutants AFF4 E61A and AFF4 K63A show a three-fold and two-fold reduction in TAR binding, respectively, while the effect of the other mutations is negligible.
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The single site mutant AFF4 K63A shows a two-fold reduction in TAR binding.
source: The single site mutants AFF4 E61A and AFF4 K63A show a three-fold and two-fold reduction in TAR binding, respectively, while the effect of the other mutations is negligible.
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The gel shift in the absence of AFF4 shows a 50-fold increased Kd for TAR binding by Tat:P-TEFb (Kd = 19 nM) compared to the gelshift in the presence of WT AFF4 (Kd = 0.26 nM).
source: The gel shift in the absence of AFF4 shows a 50-fold increased Kd for TAR binding by Tat:P-TEFb (Kd = 19 nM) compared to the gelshift in the presence of WT AFF4 (Kd = 0.26 nM).
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The small effect of surface mutations in AFF4 helix α2 on TAR binding indicates that structural stabilization of the combined interface formed collectively by Cyc T1:Tat:AFF4 is the major role of AFF4 α2.
source: The small effect of surface mutations in AFF4 helix α2 on TAR binding indicates that instead of direct interactions with TAR structural stabilization of the combined interface formed collectively by Cyc T1:Tat:AFF4 (Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014) is the major role of AFF4 α2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Wild-type AFF1 strongly supported the activation of HIV-1 LTR by Tat(C22G).
source: While wild-type AFF1 strongly supported the activation of HIV-1 LTR by Tat(C22G), all mutants displayed decreased activity, with 4-6-fold decreases observed when Glu65 (AFF4 Asp60), Glu66 (AFF4 Glu61), and Val67 (AFF4 Met62) were either singly or doubly mutated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All AFF1 mutants displayed decreased activity in supporting activation of HIV-1 LTR by Tat(C22G).
source: While wild-type AFF1 strongly supported the activation of HIV-1 LTR by Tat(C22G), all mutants displayed decreased activity, with 4-6-fold decreases observed when Glu65 (AFF4 Asp60), Glu66 (AFF4 Glu61), and Val67 (AFF4 Met62) were either singly or doubly mutated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 4-6-fold decreases in HIV-1 LTR activation were observed when AFF1 Glu65 (AFF4 Asp60), Glu66 (AFF4 Glu61), and Val67 (AFF4 Met62) were either singly or doubly mutated.
source: While wild-type AFF1 strongly supported the activation of HIV-1 LTR by Tat(C22G), all mutants displayed decreased activity, with 4-6-fold decreases observed when Glu65 (AFF4 Asp60), Glu66 (AFF4 Glu61), and Val67 (AFF4 Met62) were either singly or doubly mutated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combined results from EMSAs and transcription assays are consistent with the structural inference that AFF1/4 helix α2 plays a significant role in mediating TAR binding and Tat-transactivation, although the crystal structure shows no direct contact between them.
source: The combined results from EMSAs and transcription assays are consistent with the structural inference that AFF1/4 helix α2 plays a significant role in mediating TAR binding and Tat-transactivation, although the crystal structure shows no direct contact between them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Three TAR mutants with strongly reduced transactivation activity include G21-C41→ AU, A22-U40→ UA, and U23→C.
source: Three mutants with strongly reduced transactivation activity include G21-C41→ AU, A22-U40→ UA, and U23→C, which are located just below and in the TAR bulge.
evidence: This is based on previously published data cited in the text.

claim: In the absence of AFF4, all three TAR-mutants showed strongly reduced binding affinity compared to the WT TAR.
source: In the absence of AFF4, all three TAR-mutants showed strongly reduced binding affinity compared to the WT TAR.
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of AFF4, the affinity of WT TAR was increased 50-fold to 0.2 nM.
source: However, in the presence of AFF4, the affinity of WT TAR was increased 50-fold to 0.2 nM, and binding of the TAR-mutants was rescued to a 2–10 fold increased KD compared to WT TAR (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of AFF4, binding of the TAR-mutants was rescued to a 2–10 fold increased KD compared to WT TAR.
source: However, in the presence of AFF4, the affinity of WT TAR was increased 50-fold to 0.2 nM, and binding of the TAR-mutants was rescued to a 2–10 fold increased KD compared to WT TAR (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The potent rescue of bulge mutants by addition of AFF4 is consistent with the placement of the bulge distal to the Tat zinc-binding loops.
source: The potent rescue of bulge mutants by addition of AFF4 is consistent with the placement of the bulge distal to the Tat zinc-binding loops.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding data and the crystal structure.

claim: Nucleobases C29-G34 interact directly with the well-ordered Tat-SEC epitope consisting of the Tat zinc-binding loops and the adjacent N-terminal portion of the CycT1 TRM.
